title: Pressure-Volume Work
lead: Measuring an energy change through heat alone needs a process with no work, which for a gas means holding the volume fixed. Enthalpy is the state function defined for the easier case, a process at constant pressure.

exercise_notes: The book sets no exercises for this section; the one here is new and AI-written, its answers checked by computation with R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.source_id: That means that as long as there is no other work and we keep the pressure constant
exercises.prompt: 1.00 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is warmed by 10.0 K at constant pressure. Find (a) $\kDeltaU$ and (b) $\kDeltaH = \kqP$, in joules.

parts.hint: For a monatomic ideal gas $C_V = \tfrac{3}{2}nR$, and $C_p = C_V + nR$.

answer.solution: (a) The energy of an ideal gas depends on its temperature alone, so $\kDeltaU = \tfrac{3}{2}\knmol R\,\Delta \kT = 1.5(1.00\ \text{mol})(8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1})(10.0\ \text{K}) = 124.7$ J. (b) At constant pressure $\kDeltaH = \kqP = \kCpheat\,\Delta \kT$ with $\kCpheat = C_V + \knmol R = \tfrac{5}{2}\knmol R$, so $\kDeltaH = 2.5(1.00)(8.314)(10.0) = 207.9$ J. The extra 83.1 J is the work the gas does pushing back its surroundings as it expands.

derivations.what: the heat at constant pressure is the enthalpy change

assumes.text: The change is reversible and no work other than pressure-volume work is done.

steps.cap: With no other work, the only work is the reversible volume work.
Summed over the whole process at constant pressure, the small heats add up to $q_P$.
